title: US school-finance reforms raise long-run earnings per worker and GDP per capita after a long lag
source_unit: US state school-finance reforms, treated cohorts, earnings per worker, GDP per capita, private returns, and long-run aggregate output
geography: United States; staggered state-level school-finance reforms

observations.period: Working paper issued September 2026; state reforms and long-run cohorts

denominator.unit: US states, cohorts, workers, and state-level output; exact state and cohort counts not disclosed in the NBER abstract

simulated_earnings_10_15_years.unit: little predicted change in state-level earnings per worker during the first 10–15 years after reform

simulated_earnings_60_years.unit: percent increase in earnings per worker after 60 years in cohort-replacement simulation

observed_earnings_30_years.unit: percent increase in state-level earnings per worker above counterfactual after 30 years

gdp_per_capita_30_years.unit: more than percent increase in GDP per capita above counterfactual after 30 years

short_run_output.unit: GDP per capita declines modestly initially before rising in the long run

private_aggregate_wedge.unit: the evidence is consistent with private earnings gains aggregating to broader economic output rather than being only signaling or displacement

observations.method: The paper combines design-based micro estimates with a cohort-replacement simulation and tests the predicted path using staggered state school-finance reform implementation in an event-study framework.
observations.uncertainty: The NBER abstract does not disclose state/cohort counts, confidence intervals, exact reform features, or all event-study assumptions. Long-run aggregate estimates depend on extrapolation, cohort replacement, migration, general equilibrium, and GDP measurement; they do not establish equal gains across households or school quality in every place.
observations.subgroup: US state cohorts exposed to school-finance reforms, measured through earnings per worker and state GDP per capita over long horizons.
observations.counterinterpretation: Reforms may coincide with migration, industrial change, demographic shifts, other education policies, or selective implementation; aggregate gains can coexist with unequal local, racial, household, worker, or student outcomes.

related_sources.claim: Personalized supports for low-income students connect resources and relationships to longer-run opportunity, with implementation and outcome boundaries kept separate.
Economic connectedness is associated with substantially greater local patenting, leaving the financing-to-benefit pathway open.
Labor-force exit is concentrated among low-income and low-skill workers, illustrating why aggregate output does not equal household security.

boundary: This record adds a long-run public-investment-to-aggregate-output layer to the US education program. It does not establish equal distribution, student wellbeing, local access, worker voice, household consumption, or a complete causal pathway from reform dollars to GDP in every state.
